titre: The central pillar of Japanese pagodas does not on its own explain their earthquake resistance
accroche: In 1,400 years of seismic activity, only two Japanese pagodas are said to have collapsed because of an earthquake. The credit usually goes to a single pillar.
contenu_vulgarise:
At Hōryū-ji, near Nara, a 31.5-meter cypress pillar runs through the temple's five-story pagoda and sinks about 3 meters into the ground. The tree rings show that it comes from a tree felled in 594: it is one of the oldest worked timbers still in place in the world, in what remains the oldest standing wooden structure on Earth. This central pillar, the shinbashira, has long been presented as the reason Japanese pagodas ride out earthquakes almost without damage; in fourteen centuries, only two are said to have collapsed from this cause.

## A pillar that does not always even rest on the ground

The explanation runs up against one detail, however: the shinbashira does not always touch the ground. At Hōryū-ji, it is sunk into it. At the Nikkō Tōshōgū shrine, in its pagoda of 1818, it is instead suspended, never touching earth. Two opposite arrangements for the same intended result. Models built by engineer Shuzo Ishida offer a partial answer: a pillar anchored to the ground survives the longest, and withstands at least twice as much as a pillar hung from the fifth floor or set on a second-floor beam. But a 2010 study, which models the pillar connected to its foundation by friction supports rather than rigidly, obtains a markedly weaker seismic response than the traditional model: proof that the way the pillar is held matters at least as much as the pillar itself.

## The research is still not settled

Other mechanisms, long overshadowed by the pillar, also come into play: more recent research shows that the pagodas' very wide eaves add an inertia that also stabilizes the whole. A 1997 study looked at how this frame disperses and dissipates the earthquake's energy between the pillar and the floors, without concluding that the pillar is its only source. The encyclopedia that traces this research is blunt: the findings, by and large, “have not been very simplistic.” The principle nonetheless inspires contemporary architecture: the Tokyo Skytree, completed in 2012, incorporates a reinforced-concrete central core, decoupled from the outer frame by oil dampers above a height of 125 meters, and designed on the idea that pagodas rarely topple in an earthquake. Fourteen centuries after Hōryū-ji, we are still building on a principle we have not finished explaining.

repere.texte: The central pillar (shinbashira) of the five-story pagoda at Hōryū-ji, near Nara, comes from a tree felled in 594: it is one of the oldest worked timbers still in place in the world.

carte.punch: A single pillar does not explain why Japanese pagodas resist earthquakes.
carte.idee: The central pillar of Japanese pagodas, the shinbashira, is sunk into the ground at Hōryū-ji and suspended at Nikkō Tōshōgū: two opposite arrangements for the same result. Research adds wide eaves and energy dissipation between floors: the explanation has not been simplistic.

quiz.question: Why are researchers reluctant to attribute the earthquake resistance of Japanese pagodas solely to the central pillar (shinbashira)?
choix: Because no ancient pagoda actually has a central pillar, contrary to legend
Because models show the pillar always worsens the building's seismic response
Because the pagodas' earthquake resistance has never actually been demonstrated
Because very different pillars (sunk, suspended, friction-held) all achieve good results
quiz.explication: Sunk, suspended, or friction-connected pillars give different but all positive results according to the studies, and elements other than the pillar, such as the wide eaves, also contribute to stability: the explanation cannot be reduced to a single device. Pagodas do have a central pillar, models do not show that it worsens the seismic response, and their resistance over fourteen centuries of seismic activity is documented, not hypothetical.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the pagoda models built by engineer Shuzo Ishida show?
choix: That a central pillar anchored to the ground survives longest and withstands at least twice as much as the other arrangements tested
That a pagoda's height has no influence on its seismic resistance
That three-story pagodas resist better than five-story ones
That a central pillar worsens the seismic response beyond three stories
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ishida's models show that a pillar anchored to the ground survives longest and withstands at least twice as much as the other arrangements tested (hung from the fifth floor, or set on a second-floor beam); the other three options match no result reported by the source.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What principle inspires the central core of the Tokyo Skytree, completed in 2012?
choix: A core decoupled from the frame by dampers, modeled on the pillar of Japanese pagodas
Cross-bracing in the manner of a structural tube, as on Fazlur Khan's towers
A 1.5 cm thick concrete shell in the manner of Félix Candela
Hanging chains that calculate the shape of the structure, as with Gaudí
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Tokyo Skytree's core, decoupled from the frame by oil dampers above 125 meters, takes up the principle of the pagodas' pillar; the other three techniques belong to other stories of architecture, not to the Skytree.
